column2: The standing arrangement of heretics, guilds and the like is called samaya (agreement); breaking an agreement is remembered as a ground of dispute.
Where there are decisions about dams, fields, boundaries, ploughed and unploughed land in questions of field ownership, that is a field-born dispute.
The marriage law that is declared for women and men, called the union of woman and man, is remembered as a ground of dispute.
The division of paternal property made by sons is called inheritance, a ground of dispute according to the wise.
An act done suddenly by those proud of strength is called sahasa (violence), said to be a ground of dispute.
Abusive speech of an adverse meaning, concerning country, caste, family and the like, accompanied by limbs, is called vakparushya (verbal assault).
Injury to others' bodies with hands, feet, weapons and the like, with fire and the like, is called dandaparushya (physical assault).
Gambling with dice, rods and the like is called dyuta; with five games and living beings, it is a wager and challenge.
Miscellaneous is again known as the unsupported dispute: transgressing the king's command and not doing that act.
The legal process has eighteen grounds; their subdivisions are a hundred; by differences of men's actions it is said to have a hundred branches.
The king should see cases with learned Brahmins, without anger; assessors equal to enemy and friend, free from greed, learned in the Veda.
If he does not see because of business, he should appoint a Brahmin with the assessors. Those who act contrary to the law from passion, greed or fear,
the assessors should be fined separately, double the dispute. One who has been overpowered by others by a path contrary to law and custom,
what he reports to the king is the ground for legal proceedings. In front of the defendant it should be written as the plaintiff reported:
marked with year, month, half-month, day, name, caste and the like. The answer to the heard matter should be written in the presence of the first complainant.
The plaintiff, pressed, should have the means of proving the claimed matter recorded at once; if proved, he obtains what is proved; the reverse otherwise.
This four-footed legal procedure is shown in disputes. Without having crossed the charge one should not counter-charge him;
and one accused should not be driven into injury by another having abandoned. A counter-charge may be made in quarrels and violent acts.
A surety should be taken from both, capable, in the decision of matters of desire. In denial, when proved, he should give wealth equal to that to the king.
For a false charge double; for a charge he may take the wealth; in violence, theft and assault, in an accusation or crisis, of a woman,
one should judge at once; time is remembered otherwise by will. He goes from place to place, licks the corners of his mouth,
his forehead sweats, and his face turns pale; he goes from his nature, distorted, by deeds of mind, speech and body.
In a charge or in testimony he is called wicked of speech. One who, independent, establishes a doubtful matter and who flees,
and who, not summoned, says anything, is remembered as a wealthy fine-liable man. When witnesses are present on both sides, the earlier speakers are witnesses;
if the plaintiff's case becomes lower, they become the later speakers. If there is a dispute with a group, there the deficient one should be made to pay;
the stake given and the stake, and the wealth of the wealthy man — the king should lead the proceedings by dismissing the deceit through a messenger.
A matter even real and even stated is lost by process. One who denies all but a single thing is shown in one part;
all matters should be made to be paid by the king; one not reported is not to be taken. When two texts conflict, the rule is that of strength by procedure;
it is established that dharma-shastra is stronger than artha-shastra. Proof is declared: writing, possession, and witnesses;
in absence of any of these, one of the ordeals is said. In all disputes the later act is stronger;
in pledge, acceptance and purchase the earlier is stronger. For the owner who sees and speaks, the loss of land is of twenty years;
what is enjoyed by another, of wealth, of ten years — except pledge, boundary, deposit, and the wealth of fools and children;
and also the wealth of deposits, the king, women and Shrotriyas. One who withholds pledges and the like should be made to pay wealth to the owner,
and a fine equal to the king, or according to ability. Title is greater than possession received by earlier succession;
but title too is not strong where there is not even a little possession. With pure title, enjoyment reaches proof;
enjoyment with impure title does not reach authority. The one who made the title, the accused, should clear him;
not his son or his son's son; there possession is heavier. One accused who has died, from his estate one should clear him;
there possession without title is not a cause. One should revoke transactions done by force or deceit:
done by women, at night, inside the house, outside the house, by enemies, and prompted by the drunk, mad, ill, addicted, child or frightened,
and done unconnectedly — such a transaction is not valid. Lost property should be given by the king to the owner, up to a hundred,
and if he does not establish by marks, he should give the equivalent; stolen property should be restored by the king to the district;
interest is an eightieth part each month with security; by order of castes a hundred, two, three, four, five;
seventy for cattle and women; for juices eightfold beyond; for cloth, grain and gold fourfold, threefold, twofold;
ten from another village; twenty even by sea. Or all should give the interest they themselves made, in all castes.
One who has fled while accomplishing his matter should not be spoken to; if the king is approached while being settled, he is punished and made to pay that wealth.
When the father has gone abroad, died, or been overwhelmed by distress, the debt is to be paid by sons and grandsons, when denied established by witnesses;
what was incurred for liquor, lust, gambling, the remainder of fines and tolls, and a gift made in vain — a son should not pay these as paternal.
For brothers, for a married pair, for father and son, suretyship and debt are remembered as to be taken by the undivided;
suretyship is ordained for appearance, credit and payment. In a pledge when it is false the sons of the false one are to be made to pay;
where the surety for appearance has died, or the credit surety, his sons need not pay the wealth; those standing for payment should pay.
If there are many, the sureties should pay the wealth by their own shares; among those under one shelter, as the creditor pleases.
Where a surety has been made to pay publicly wealth to the owner, the debtors should repay it double to him.
Grain for one's own offspring, women and cattle is double; cloth is said fourfold and juice eightfold.
The pledge is lost when the wealth has doubled, if not released; at the time what is done by time is lost; the one enjoying the fruit does not lose.
A pledge to be kept is enjoyed without interest; in what is done with service and established, lost or destroyed, it should be paid except by fate or king.
By acceptance of a pledge it is settled; even guarded, if it goes worthless, another pledge may be given, or the owner becomes a sharer of wealth;
conduct made by the mortgagee should be made to pay with interest; the wealth made by a true pledge should be repaid double.
The pledge should be released to the one who presents himself, otherwise a fine; if there is a lender, the wealth should be obtained from another's family;
or its price made at that time, he should stay there without interest; or without a holder he may sell with witnesses.
When the debt has become double on the pledge, then the pledge should be released, producing it, when double the wealth has entered.
What substance one entrusts into another's hand, being in distress, without telling, that is a deposit, to be returned likewise.
It is not to be paid if taken by king, fate or thieves; if sent away when asked and given, he should pay and a fine equal to it;
one who lives on it at will should be fined and made to pay it with interest. This rule is also in borrowed, lent, trust and deposit.
The defeat of one who speaks otherwise is certain; even when stated, if in testimony by witnesses others more qualified
or twofold say otherwise, the former witnesses are false. The false-doers and witnesses should be fined separately;
a fine double the dispute; a Brahmin is remembered as to be banished. One who, having been made to hear testimony, denies it from others, covered by darkness,
he should be made to pay an eightfold fine; a Brahmin he should banish. Where there is death of castemen, there a witness may speak untruth.
Whatever matter is agreed mutually by their own wish, a document with witnesses should be made, owner first,
marked with year, month, day, name, caste and own clan, fellow student, self, father's name and so on.
At the end of the matter the debtor should enter in his own hand his name: "This is approved by me, son of so-and-so, what is written above."
The witnesses too in their own hand, with father's name first: "Here I, so-and-so, am witness" — they should write, they being equal.
A debtor who does not know writing should have his agreement written; or a witness by another witness in presence of all witnesses;
Requested by both, this was written by me, son of so-and-so — the scribe finally should write.
Even without witnesses, a document written in one's own hand is all proof, except what is made by force or deceit.
A debt recorded in a document is to be paid by three generations only; the pledge is enjoyed as long as it is not paid.
